## Why examine recurrence?

My PhD research uses ambient-vibration evidence to help characterize
buildings affected by earthquakes. One useful review question is whether
similar candidate frequencies appear in different portions of a recording.

Here, I examine frequency families assembled from early, middle, and late
recording windows. A family groups nearby candidate frequencies within
one building case. Recurrence can help prioritize further review, but it
does not by itself confirm a structural mode.

## Data source and scope

The data come from the `FAMILIES` sheet of my
`RECoVER_FieldAV_AdjudicationWorkbook_AR38D.xlsx` research workbook.

The [frequency-family CSV](field-av-frequency-families.csv) contains
the selected fields used in this analysis, including building identifiers,
frequency summaries, window counts, and review flags.

Each row represents one candidate frequency family, not one building.
These are processed research records, rather than raw sensor measurements.
The source workbook marks every family as not automatically accepted.

This preliminary research sample is shared to demonstrate a reproducible
analysis workflow for DSCI 521 Milestone 3 and my research portfolio.
It represents a selected workbook snapshot, rather than the complete
or final research dataset. The results describe this sample and should
not be interpreted as final thesis findings.

## Load the packages

I use pandas for reading and summarizing the records and matplotlib
for the figure.

```{python}
#| label: setup

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display
```

## Read and check the records

I check the fields required for this analysis, verify that family
identifiers are unique within each case, and confirm that window counts
fall within the three recording windows.

```{python}
#| label: inspect-frequency-families

families = pd.read_csv("field-av-frequency-families.csv")

required = [
    "CaseID",
    "FamilyID",
    "FrequencyMedian_Hz",
    "WindowsRepresented",
    "RelativeFrequencySpread_pct",
]

assert families[required].notna().all().all()
assert not families.duplicated(["CaseID", "FamilyID"]).any()
assert families["WindowsRepresented"].isin([1, 2, 3]).all()
assert families["FrequencyMedian_Hz"].gt(0).all()
assert families["RelativeFrequencySpread_pct"].ge(0).all()

overview = pd.DataFrame({
    "Frequency families": [len(families)],
    "Building cases": [families["CaseID"].nunique()],
    "Missing required values": [
        families[required].isna().sum().sum()
    ],
})

display(overview)
```

This snapshot contains 87 candidate frequency families across 13
building cases. Multiple families can belong to the same building.

The externally analysed case TK3144-12 is absent from this automatic
family table. Its absence does not mean that the building has no
vibration modes.

## Count recurrence across windows

I count how many families appear in one, two, or all three windows.
The percentage denominator is the total number of families.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-window-recurrence

recurrence = (
    families["WindowsRepresented"]
    .value_counts()
    .reindex([1, 2, 3], fill_value=0)
    .rename_axis("Windows represented")
    .reset_index(name="Frequency families")
)

recurrence["Percentage of families"] = (
    100 * recurrence["Frequency families"] / len(families)
).round(1)

display(recurrence)
```

There are 42 families represented in one window, 26 in two windows,
and 19 in all three. Therefore, 45 of the 87 families appear in at
least two windows.

These are family-level counts. Buildings contributing more families
have more influence on this summary.

## Visualize recurrence

The figure shows the number of families in each recurrence category.
Integer labels above the bars make the counts explicit.

```{python}
#| label: fig-window-recurrence
#| fig-cap: "Candidate frequency families represented in one, two, or three recording windows. Counts refer to families, not buildings."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

bars = ax.bar(
    recurrence["Windows represented"],
    recurrence["Frequency families"],
    color="#2563EB",
)

ax.bar_label(bars, padding=3)
ax.set(
    xticks=[1, 2, 3],
    xlabel="Number of recording windows represented",
    ylabel="Number of candidate frequency families",
    ylim=(0, 50),
)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Examine frequency spread among recurring families

Recurrence and frequency spread describe different aspects of the
evidence. A family can recur across windows while its candidate
frequencies vary.

For this comparison, I retain families represented in at least two
windows. A family containing only one candidate necessarily has zero
observed spread, which would not demonstrate repeatability.

I summarize the workbook's recorded relative frequency spread.
The values are percentages, not confidence intervals.

```{python}
#| label: summarize-frequency-spread

repeated = families.loc[
    families["WindowsRepresented"] >= 2
]

spread_summary = (
    repeated.groupby("WindowsRepresented")[
        "RelativeFrequencySpread_pct"
    ]
    .agg(["count", "median", "min", "max"])
    .rename(columns={
        "count": "Families",
        "median": "Median spread (%)",
        "min": "Minimum spread (%)",
        "max": "Maximum spread (%)",
    })
    .rename_axis("Windows represented")
    .reset_index()
    .round(2)
)

display(spread_summary)
```

The median recorded spread is approximately 1.77% for families
represented in two windows and 3.39% for families represented in
three windows.

This comparison involves different sets of families. It does not
show that adding a window causes a larger spread. The grouping rule
and number of candidate observations also affect the summaries.

## What does this mean for my research?

In this snapshot, just over half of the candidate frequency families
appear in more than one recording window. These recurring families
provide a useful starting point for closer review.

However, the windows come from the same building recordings and
are not independent building observations. Recurrence alone cannot
identify a frequency as a translational or torsional structural mode.

For my RECoVER workflow, this analysis documents the available
candidate evidence before reviewing directions, mode shapes, and
other diagnostics. Final modal selections remain a separate task.
